name: Takayama and Shirakawa-go
tagline: Old mountain streets, thatched farmhouse villages, and Hida beef
intro: Base yourself in Takayama, a town that still keeps its Edo-period streets, and take day trips to the UNESCO World Heritage village of Shirakawa-go, the Shin-Hotaka Ropeway in the Northern Alps, and the Gero and Hirayu hot springs. Walking distances are short and buses connect everything, so it works well with parents or kids, and you can enjoy Hida beef prepared a different way at every meal. Fly into Nagoya (NGO) or Toyama (TOY) and ride the Limited Express Hida up into the mountains.
season_notes: Spring (Apr-May): the Spring Takayama Festival runs April 14-15, cherry blossoms bloom in mid-April with leftover snow at Shirakawa-go, and Kamikochi opens in late April. Summer (Jun-Sep): the mountains are cooler than the cities, though midday is still hot; August, after the rainy season (mid-June to mid-July), is the best time for the ropeway. Autumn (Oct-Nov): the Autumn Takayama Festival is October 9-10, fall color peaks at Shin-Hotaka in mid-October, and at Shirakawa-go and the old town in early November. Winter (Dec-Feb): snow-covered thatched houses and light-up events in January and February (reservation required), plus the snow corridor at the ropeway; just allow for bus delays and slippery roads.
airport_access/0/mode: Meitetsu mu-SKY + JR Limited Express Hida
airport_access/0/note: mu-SKY 28 min, about ¥1,250 (to be confirmed) → change at Nagoya Station → Limited Express Hida 2 hr 30 min, ¥6,340 (reserved seat). About 3 hr 10 min including a 30-minute transfer
airport_access/1/note: Express bus from Meitetsu Bus Center in Nagoya, 2 hr 45 min, about ¥3,400 (to be confirmed). Cheaper than the train, reservation required. Whether a direct airport-to-Takayama bus runs is to be confirmed
airport_access/2/mode: Airport bus + JR Limited Express Hida
airport_access/2/note: Airport bus to Toyama Station 25 min, about ¥420 (to be confirmed) → Limited Express Hida 1 hr 30 min, about ¥3,500 (to be confirmed). Service is infrequent, so check the timetable
getting_around: The sights in central Takayama (old town, Takayama Jinya, morning markets, Yatai Kaikan) are all within a 15-minute walk of the station. Hida no Sato is a 10-minute ride on the Sarubobo Bus from the station, and buses to Shirakawa-go, Hirayu, Shin-Hotaka and Nagoya all leave from the Nohi Bus Center next to the station. If you stay near the station, you can make a bus trip out and back each day. Many Shirakawa-go buses are reservation-only, so book on the Nohibus website by the day before. IC cards work only on JR and some Nohi buses, so carry cash.
transport_pass: Only for the Okuhida area, the Takayama-Shin-Hotaka 2-Day Pass at about ¥4,400 (to be confirmed) beats buying round trips. For Shirakawa-go there is a round-trip ticket discount (to be confirmed), and you will walk around town, so no other pass is needed. Work out whether a JR pass (such as the Takayama-Hokuriku Pass) pays off only if you are also adding Kanazawa or Toyama.
spots/0/desc: An international airport on an artificial island off Nagoya, with direct flights from Incheon and Gimhae. Sky Town on the 4th floor has restaurants and an observation deck, a nice way to pass time before your flight.
spots/0/access: Meitetsu trains (mu-SKY or limited express) or express buses from the 2nd-floor Transport Plaza
spots/0/hours: Shops and restaurants generally 7:00–21:00 (to be confirmed)
spots/0/tip: To reach Takayama, take Meitetsu to Nagoya Station, then change to the JR Limited Express Hida or an express bus. Allow a generous 30 minutes for the transfer at Nagoya Station.
spots/0/kid_tip: The 4th-floor observation deck lets you watch planes take off and land up close, and the Fuji Dream Airlines museum (annex) is popular with kids.
spots/1/desc: A small airport close to central Toyama with a few direct flights a week from Incheon. The airport bus reaches Toyama Station in 25 minutes, and from there the JR Limited Express Hida takes 1 hr 30 min to Takayama.
spots/1/access: Airport bus from the front of the 1st-floor arrivals lobby to Toyama Station
spots/1/tip: You can also fly into Toyama, pass through Takayama, and fly out of Nagoya (NGO). Direct flights are few, so lock in your flight schedule first.
spots/2/desc: The transfer station where you change from the Meitetsu line to the JR Limited Express Hida or the express buses. Meitetsu Nagoya Station and JR Nagoya Station are linked underground, a 5-7 minute walk, and express buses leave from the Meitetsu Bus Center in front of the station (floors 3-4 of the Meitetsu Department Store).
spots/2/access: Meitetsu Nagoya Station → JR central ticket gate, 7 min on foot
spots/2/tip: Reserved seats are the safe choice on the Limited Express Hida. Buy them by the day before on the JR Central website (Smart EX / EX Reservation) or at the station's Green Window. For a train lunch box, try the Grand Kiosk inside the JR gates.
spots/2/kid_tip: Kids love the front-facing observation seats (Car 1) on the Hida train, but they sell out early.
spots/3/name: Takayama Station and Nohi Bus Center
spots/3/desc: The central station of this trip. Buses to Shirakawa-go, Shin-Hotaka, Hirayu Onsen and Nagoya all leave from the Nohi Bus Center right next to it, and the old town is a 12-minute walk from the east exit.
spots/3/access: JR Takayama Main Line, terminus of the Limited Express Hida
spots/3/hours: Open 24 hours (bus center ticket windows about 6:00–19:00, to be confirmed)
spots/3/tip: Many Shirakawa-go buses are reservation-only. Book ahead on the Nohibus website and keep the QR code handy. Coin lockers are in the station and at the bus center.
spots/4/desc: Three lanes of Edo-period merchant houses make up the face of Takayama. Cedar balls (sugidama) hang from sake brewery eaves, and shops selling mitarashi dango and Hida beef sushi and lattice-windowed tea houses are packed into one neighborhood, so just wandering takes half a day.
spots/4/access: 12 min on foot from Takayama Station east exit
spots/4/hours: Shops generally 9:00–17:00, and most close in the evening
spots/4/tip: It is quietest before 9 a.m. and after 4 p.m. Sake breweries (Harada, Funasaka and others) charge a few hundred yen for tastings and give you a cup. The street goes dark early in the evening, so don't expect a night view.
spots/4/kid_tip: It is a street of snacks, so kids don't get bored. The lanes are narrow and cars pass through, so hold their hands.
spots/5/desc: A market held every morning along the Miyagawa River, the symbol of a Takayama morning. About 300 m of stalls sell farmers' pickles, apples and hoba miso, handmade sarubobo dolls, freshly baked rice crackers, and coffee from food carts.
spots/5/access: 10 min on foot from Takayama Station, right next to Sanmachi
spots/5/hours: 7:00–12:00 (from 8:00 from December to March); stalls are liveliest before 10
spots/5/tip: Bring small bills for cash. Stalls start packing up after 10, so around 8 a.m. is best, as a breakfast stop too.
spots/5/kid_tip: Picking out a sarubobo doll and sharing an apple juice is plenty of fun.
spots/6/desc: A produce market held in the square in front of the Takayama Jinya main gate. It is smaller than the Miyagawa market and centers on vegetables, pickles and flowers, so it feels more local.
spots/6/access: 10 min on foot from Takayama Station
spots/6/tip: Make a loop before the Jinya opens (8:45) and walk straight in for a tidy route.
spots/7/desc: The former government office from which the Edo shogunate ruled the Hida region directly, and the only such magistrate's building still standing in Japan. The offices, interrogation room and even the rice storehouse remain, and the long tatami corridors make it a good indoor visit on a rainy day.
spots/7/access: 10 min on foot from Takayama Station
spots/7/hours: 8:45–17:00 (16:30 from November to March; last entry 30 min before closing)
spots/7/tip: Admission is about ¥500 for adults (to be confirmed) and free for high school students and younger. If a free volunteer guide is available, take the explanation. You remove your shoes, so wear socks.
spots/7/kid_tip: The stone-weight torture tools in the interrogation room may need some explaining to a child. The wide tatami corridors are pleasant to walk.
spots/8/desc: A red-railed bridge over the Miyagawa, a favorite backdrop for Takayama photos. It pairs with cherry blossoms on both banks in spring and with fall color in autumn, and the festival floats (yatai) cross this bridge during the Takayama Festival.
spots/8/access: 2 min on foot from the Jinya
spots/8/tip: Take your photos before 8 a.m. when there are no crowds. West of the bridge is the Jinya, east is Sanmachi.
spots/9/name: Sakurayama Hachimangu Shrine and Takayama Festival Float Exhibition Hall (Yatai Kaikan)
spots/9/desc: A hall with a permanent display of the festival floats (yatai) that star in the Autumn Takayama Festival (October 9-10). Four floats, packed with gold leaf and carvings, are shown in rotation, and the quiet grounds of Hachimangu Shrine next door make a nice stroll.
spots/9/tip: The ticket is shared with the neighboring Sakurayama Nikkokan (a model of Nikko Toshogu Shrine), about ¥1,000 (to be confirmed). Outside the festival days, this is the only place to see the floats.
spots/9/kid_tip: A video shows the puppet-show mechanism on top of the floats.
spots/10/desc: An open-air museum of more than 30 gassho-zukuri farmhouses relocated onto a hillside around a pond. It makes a good substitute on a day you can't get to Shirakawa-go, and craft demonstrations in the houses (straw sandals, lacquerware) keep kids from getting bored.
spots/10/access: 10 min by Sarubobo Bus from in front of Takayama Station, or 10 min by taxi
spots/10/tip: ¥700 for adults, ¥200 for elementary and junior high students. A combo ticket bundling the round-trip bus from the station with admission is available (to be confirmed). The winter evening light-up, with snow-covered thatched houses, is spectacular.
spots/10/kid_tip: Feed the pond carp and try the irori (hearth) in a farmhouse. Strollers are tough on the gravel paths.
spots/11/desc: A 3.5 km walking path lined with a dozen or so temples and shrines on the hill east of the old town. It is compared to Kyoto's Philosopher's Path but is far quieter, and it ends at Shiroyama Park, the site of Takayama Castle.
spots/11/tip: The full route is long, so rather than walking all of it, a 1 km stretch behind Sanmachi around Soyuji (素玄寺) and Daioji gives you plenty of atmosphere. There are some uphill sections, so wear sneakers.
spots/12/desc: A 1,200-year-old temple between the station and the old town, known for its three-story pagoda and a 1,250-year-old ginkgo tree. The grounds are small, so you can see them in 10 minutes on the way past.
spots/12/access: 5 min on foot from Takayama Station
spots/12/tip: The grounds are free, and entering the main hall costs about ¥300 (to be confirmed). It is prettiest in mid-November when yellow ginkgo leaves carpet the ground.
spots/13/desc: A private museum that recreates an entire Japanese shopping street of the 1950s and 60s. You can go inside and touch things in an old classroom, barbershop and electronics shop, so it is a good way to spend an hour with kids on a rainy day.
spots/13/tip: Admission is about ¥1,000 for adults (to be confirmed). A shop selling old-fashioned candy and toys at the entrance is great for nostalgic souvenirs.
spots/13/kid_tip: Take photos at the old game machines and classroom desks. Children's admission is cheap.
spots/14/name: Hida Takayama Teddy Bear Eco Village
spots/14/desc: A teddy bear museum in a converted gassho-zukuri farmhouse, right next to Hida no Sato. With over 1,000 teddy bears and a cafe, it combines with Hida no Sato for a half-day outing.
spots/14/access: 3 min on foot from Hida no Sato
spots/14/tip: Admission is about ¥600 (to be confirmed). The cafe's cookies and latte art make good photo spots.
spots/14/kid_tip: If you have kids, be sure to stop here after Hida no Sato. There is also a teddy bear making workshop (to be confirmed).
spots/15/desc: A UNESCO World Heritage village of gassho-zukuri farmhouses. More than 100 steep-roofed, thatched houses are scattered between rice paddies and the river, and because people still live here, simply walking the lanes takes half a day.
spots/15/access: 50 min to 1 hr 10 min by bus from Takayama Nohi Bus Center
spots/15/tip: From the bus terminal, cross the Deai Bridge suspension bridge to enter the village. Do not enter residents' homes or yards. The winter light-up (specific days in January and February) requires advance reservations.
spots/15/kid_tip: Kids love the swaying suspension bridge. Cars use the village roads, so be careful.
spots/16/desc: A hilltop viewpoint overlooking the whole village, where the postcard photos are taken. It is a 15-20 minute uphill walk from the village, and a shuttle bus also runs.
spots/16/access: 15 min on foot via the trail behind the Wada house, or by shuttle bus (fare to be confirmed)
spots/16/tip: The shuttle runs about every 20 minutes, but reports conflict on whether it is paid or free, so confirm on site. The walking trail is slippery in snow or rain. Mornings have less backlight.
spots/17/desc: The largest gassho-zukuri house in the village, an Important Cultural Property. Silkworm-raising tools remain in the 2nd- and 3rd-floor lofts, and the views of the village through the windows are lovely.
spots/17/access: 5 min on foot from Shirakawa-go Bus Terminal
spots/17/tip: ¥400 for adults, ¥200 for elementary students. The Kanda house (神田家) and Nagase house (長瀬家) cost the same, so if you choose just one, pick Wada; if two, add Kanda (they serve a cup of tea).
spots/17/kid_tip: Hold your child's hand on the steep loft stairs.
spots/18/desc: An open-air museum across the river from the village with 25 relocated and restored gassho-zukuri houses. Nobody lives here, so you can freely walk in and out of the houses, and there is a soba shop and craft workshops.
spots/18/access: Right across the Deai Bridge suspension bridge
spots/18/hours: 8:40–17:00 (9:00–16:00 from December to March, to be confirmed)
spots/18/closed: Thursdays from December to March (to be confirmed)
spots/18/tip: Admission is about ¥600 (to be confirmed). When the main village is crowded, this is actually a better place to see the inside of gassho houses in peace.
spots/18/kid_tip: Straw craft workshop (no reservation needed, to be confirmed).
spots/19/desc: A small terminal where buses to Takayama, Kanazawa and Toyama gather, with a tourist information office, coin lockers and restrooms. It is a 3-minute walk to the suspension bridge at the village entrance.
spots/19/tip: Many return buses require a reservation. Leave luggage in the terminal lockers (about ¥700 for large bags).
spots/20/desc: The station of a hot spring town where the Limited Express Hida stops, between Takayama and Nagoya. There is a foot bath in front of the station, the hot spring street is a 10-minute walk, and most inn shuttles come to the station.
spots/20/access: JR Takayama Main Line, Limited Express Hida stop
spots/20/tip: If you get off here for a night between Nagoya and Takayama, it adds almost nothing to your transport cost. Put large bags in the station lockers.
spots/21/desc: A small folk village with 10 gassho-zukuri houses moved from Shirakawa-go. It has a 175 m slide, pottery painting and papermaking workshops, so it is a great place to spend time with kids.
spots/21/access: 20 min on foot or 6 min by bus from Gero Station
spots/21/tip: ¥800 for adults, ¥400 for elementary and junior high students. Workshops cost extra (painting from ¥1,300). It is on a hill, so the way back is downhill.
spots/21/kid_tip: Adults ride the 175 m slide too. Gloves are provided.
spots/22/name: Gero Onsen Street and Shirasagi no Yu
spots/22/desc: An alkaline hot spring town counted among Japan's three famous springs. More than nine foot baths are scattered along the river, and the public bath Shirasagi no Yu and shops selling onsen eggs and pudding are within walking distance.
spots/22/access: 10 min on foot from Gero Station
spots/22/hours: Foot baths open 24 hours; Shirasagi no Yu 10:00–22:00 (to be confirmed)
spots/22/closed: Shirasagi no Yu closed Wednesdays (to be confirmed)
spots/22/tip: The Yumeguri Tegata (a pass for three baths) costs about ¥1,500 (to be confirmed) and lets you bathe at inns even if you aren't staying overnight. Bring a towel for the foot baths.
spots/22/kid_tip: Foot baths are free, so they are easy to tour with kids. At the riverside open-air bath Fusenchi, swimsuits are required.
spots/23/desc: A free open-air bath ringed with stones in the middle of the Hida River, the iconic view of Gero Onsen. Swimsuits have been mandatory since the late 2010s, and recent notices say it has shifted to mostly foot-bath use, so check current conditions on site (to be confirmed).
spots/23/tip: There are no changing rooms, so put your swimsuit on at your inn before you go. The view from the bridge is nice on its own.
spots/24/desc: Japan's only double-decker gondola, climbing to Nishi-Hotakaguchi Station at 2,156 m. The summit observatory gives a 360-degree panorama of the Northern Alps peaks, and in winter the snow corridor and snowy viewing deck are magnificent.
spots/24/access: 1 hr 30 min by bus from Takayama Nohi Bus Center (a one-way option via Hirayu transfer is available)
spots/24/hours: 8:30–16:00 for uphill departures (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/24/closed: Bad weather and maintenance days (suspended for periods in April and November, to be confirmed)
spots/24/tip: Round trip on Ropeways 1 and 2 combined is ¥3,800 for adults and ¥1,900 for children. The summit is about 10 degrees cooler than below, so bring a jacket even in summer. There is less cloud in the morning.
spots/24/kid_tip: The midway Shirakabadaira Station has a foot bath and a bakery, and the rooftop observatory at the top station has railings for safety.
spots/25/name: Hirayu Onsen and Hirayu no Mori
spots/25/desc: A hot spring town between Takayama and Shin-Hotaka and Kamikochi, and a bus transfer hub. Hirayu no Mori, right next to the bus terminal, is a day-use onsen with 16 open-air baths for about ¥700, a great stop on the way back from the ropeway.
spots/25/access: 1 hr by bus from Takayama Nohi Bus Center
spots/25/tip: Towels are available for a rental fee. Eating a Hida beef rice bowl at the restaurant on the bus terminal's 2nd floor before you bathe makes the route work smoothly. Check the last bus back to Takayama first.
spots/25/kid_tip: Hirayu no Mori has low kids' prices and some shallow baths. The floors are slippery, so watch out for sandals.
spots/26/desc: A Northern Alps mountain resort 25 minutes by bus from Hirayu, open only from mid-April to November 15. The classic outing is to look up at the Hotaka range from Kappabashi Bridge and walk the flat forest path to Taisho Pond.
spots/26/access: 25 min by shuttle bus from Hirayu Bus Terminal (private cars not allowed)
spots/26/hours: Mid-April to November 15; first bus around 5 a.m., last bus around 5 p.m. (to be confirmed)
spots/26/tip: The round-trip bus between Hirayu and Kamikochi is about ¥2,800 (to be confirmed). As a day trip from Takayama, doing it on the same day as Shin-Hotaka is tight, so choose just one.
spots/26/kid_tip: The 3.5 km flat walk from Taisho Pond to Kappabashi is manageable for kids. Monkeys often appear, so don't show them food.
spots/27/desc: A small old town 15 minutes by train from Takayama, known for its white-walled storehouses and the Setogawa Canal where carp swim. It is known as a setting for the film Your Name., and with few tourists it is a quiet place to walk.
spots/27/access: 15 min by local train or 12 min by limited express from JR Takayama Station
spots/27/hours: Open 24 hours (Festival Hall 9:00–17:00, to be confirmed)
spots/27/tip: Pick up a free map of the film's scenes at the tourist information office in front of the station. From December to March the carp are moved to winter ponds and are not in the canal.
restaurants/0/signature: Assorted Hida beef yakiniku set meal
restaurants/0/desc: A restaurant run directly by a Hida beef butcher, so you can eat the same grade of beef for less than elsewhere in town. The 1st floor is a butcher counter and bento shop, and the 2nd-floor dining room focuses on yakiniku and hoba miso grilled set meals.
restaurants/0/tips/0: Lunch sets are 30% cheaper than dinner
restaurants/0/tips/1: Table seating for families with kids
restaurants/0/tips/2: Take a waiting number on the 1st floor
restaurants/1/desc: Takayama's signature steakhouse, open since 1964. It is known for its teppan-grilled course and beef stew, and the Western-style tables are comfortable for older guests and families with kids.
restaurants/1/tips/0: The lunch steak set costs half the dinner price
restaurants/1/tips/1: Reservations recommended on weekends and evenings
restaurants/2/desc: The Sanmachi street stall with the longest line for beef sushi. Lightly seared Hida beef sushi is served on a rice cracker plate, about ¥1,000 for 2-3 pieces, great for a snack on your stroll.
restaurants/2/tips/0: The line is shorter before 11 a.m.
restaurants/2/tips/1: The plate is a rice cracker too, so no trash
restaurants/3/desc: A handmade burger shop in a converted old house, famous for its Hida beef patty burger. The English menu and relaxed atmosphere draw many foreign visitors and families, and there are small burgers for kids.
restaurants/3/tips/0: Arrive before noon to beat the lunch peak
restaurants/3/tips/2: Few seats, so waits are common
restaurants/4/desc: The original Takayama ramen shop, which started as a street cart in 1938. A bowl of soy-based broth with thin curly noodles is about ¥900, a good early lunch after the morning market.
restaurants/4/hours: 11:00–15:00 (closes when sold out, to be confirmed)
restaurants/4/tips/1: The only menu item is ramen
restaurants/5/signature: Hoba miso set meal and Hida beef sukiyaki
restaurants/5/desc: A farmhouse-style restaurant with an irori hearth serving set meals of hoba miso, mountain vegetables and Hida beef. It is on the way to the Yatai Kaikan, so it pairs well with the Hachiman area.
restaurants/5/tips/2: Single set meals can be ordered
restaurants/6/cuisine: Hida beef rice bowl and beef sushi
restaurants/6/desc: An old restaurant in the middle of Sanmachi that sells beef sushi at the storefront and beef rice bowls and soba inside. It is a solid choice when you need a place to sit down and eat during your old town walk.
restaurants/6/tips/0: Expect a wait during the 12-1 p.m. lunch peak
restaurants/6/tips/1: Beef sushi can be taken out
restaurants/7/desc: A small Chinese restaurant run by an elderly couple, known among foreign travelers for its separate vegetarian and vegan menu. The gyoza and fried rice suit kids' tastes and prices are low.
restaurants/7/tips/0: Only about 10 seats, so expect a wait
restaurants/8/desc: A long-established Takayama ramen shop, ranked alongside Masago Soba. The broth is a little richer, and choices like chashu-men and wonton-men let everyone in the family order their own.
restaurants/8/tips/1: Mostly counter seating, so strollers are difficult
restaurants/9/signature: Hida milk pudding and pumpkin pudding
restaurants/9/desc: A pudding shop run by the French restaurant Le Midi next to Nakabashi Bridge. It sells Hida milk pudding and Shukuné pumpkin pudding to take out, a good sugar boost on your stroll.
restaurants/9/tips/0: If you buy bottled puddings, you need a cooler bag
restaurants/9/tips/1: Eat them on a nearby bench
restaurants/9/tips/2: The main Le Midi restaurant serves Hida beef French cuisine
restaurants/10/cuisine: Tea house and sweet red bean treats
restaurants/10/signature: Matcha warabimochi and sweet red bean soup
restaurants/10/desc: A tea house in a lattice-windowed house right in the middle of Sanmachi. Sitting on the floor at the back, looking at the garden with warabimochi and matcha, completes the old town atmosphere.
restaurants/10/tips/0: Take off your shoes to enter
restaurants/11/desc: A yakiniku restaurant right in front of Takayama Station, convenient for dinner on a late-arrival day. It offers Hida beef assortments by grade and offal, with table seating and good smoke ventilation.
restaurants/12/signature: Hoba miso set meal and salt-grilled iwana
restaurants/12/desc: Shirakawa-go's signature restaurant, where you eat beside an irori hearth inside a gassho-zukuri house. Its specialties are a set meal of hoba miso topped with Hida beef and salt-grilled iwana (river char), and lines are long around lunchtime.
restaurants/13/signature: Unlimited refills of zenzai (sweet red bean soup) and curry
restaurants/13/desc: A gassho-style cafe deep in the village that offers refills of sweet red bean soup from a pot hanging over the irori. It is good for warming up in winter, and the curry makes a light lunch.
restaurants/13/tips/0: Few seats, so expect a wait
restaurants/13/tips/2: Refills of the red bean soup are allowed
restaurants/14/signature: Salt-grilled iwana and trout set meal
restaurants/14/desc: A restaurant next to a fish farm at the southern end of the village that grills its own iwana and trout. It is quieter than the center, so it is good for a relaxed meal with kids.
restaurants/14/tips/0: 15 min on foot from the village entrance
restaurants/15/signature: Onsen egg soft serve and onsen pudding
restaurants/15/desc: A cafe and souvenir shop in the middle of Gero's hot spring street. The classic move is to soak your feet in the foot bath out front while eating an onsen tamago soft serve.
restaurants/16/desc: A specialist in keichan, the local Gero dish of seasoned grilled chicken. It is a simple meal of chicken and cabbage stir-fried on an iron griddle, eaten with rice, and it is a 10-minute walk from Gero Station.
restaurants/17/signature: Hida beef hoba miso set meal and keichan
restaurants/17/desc: A local restaurant near the Hirayu Onsen bus terminal, convenient for lunch on the way back from the ropeway. It has hoba miso set meals and mountain vegetable soba, with roomy seating.
restaurants/17/tips/0: Order ahead to match your bus time
restaurants/18/signature: Zaru soba and Hida beef soba
restaurants/18/desc: A handmade soba shop in the old town of Hida-Furukawa. It is a good stop after strolling the Setogawa Canal, and besides soba it also serves a beef rice bowl.
restaurants/19/desc: A stand-up kishimen noodle shop on the Shinkansen and conventional line platforms at Nagoya Station. You can eat in 10 minutes before boarding the Limited Express Hida, perfect for a transfer lunch.
restaurants/19/hours: About 7:00–21:00 (varies by platform, to be confirmed)
restaurants/19/tips/1: On the platform, so go after passing the ticket gate
restaurants/20/desc: The Nagoya Station underground mall (Esca) branch of the famous Nagoya miso katsu chain. It is a 5-minute walk from Meitetsu Nagoya Station, so it is easy to have lunch on your way up from the airport before boarding the Hida train.
hotels/0/name: Hida Hanasato no Yu Takayama Sakuraan
hotels/0/desc: A 3-minute walk from the station, with tatami floors in every room and a rooftop natural hot spring open-air bath. It offers free late-night ramen and a breakfast buffet with Hida beef dishes, making it the most efficient choice for a short trip.
hotels/0/pts/0: 3 min on foot to the station and bus center
hotels/0/pts/1: Rooftop open-air bath with night view
hotels/1/desc: A high-end ryokan right in front of Takayama Jinya, serving Hida beef in its kaiseki dinner. With few rooms it is quiet, and it has a women-only hot spring called Rirakusu.
hotels/1/pts/0: 2 min on foot to the old town and Jinya
hotels/2/desc: A large resort hotel on a hill west of the city, where the scenic hot spring bath looks out on the Northern Alps. A free shuttle runs to the station and the rooms are spacious, which suits family trips.
hotels/3/desc: A business hotel 3 minutes on foot from the station with a rooftop hot spring bath. The breakfast and hot spring are good for the price, so it suits solo travelers or couples staying simply.
hotels/3/pts/0: 3 min on foot to the station
hotels/4/desc: A large ryokan representing Gero Onsen, 3 minutes on foot from the station. Its three wings each have a different large bath, so you can make a bath tour of it, and children's rates and a Western restaurant make it easy for families.
hotels/4/pts/0: 3 min on foot to the station

variants/2/title: Plan with Kids (Hida no Sato and Gero Gassho Village)
variants/2/theme: Less walking, more hands-on activities, 2 nights
variants/2/summary: A 2-night trip built around Hida no Sato, the Teddy Bear museum and Showa-kan in Takayama and the slide at Gero Gassho Village, in place of Shirakawa-go. Lodging is fixed at a family resort with a station shuttle.

variants/2/days/1/note: Hida no Sato in the morning (pond carp and straw crafts), the Teddy Bear museum next door, then old toys at Showa-kan after lunch. The walking distance is short.

bplan/0/title: Indoors on rainy days: Jinya, Showa-kan and Yatai Kaikan
bplan/0/desc: If rain makes Shirakawa-go or Shin-Hotaka difficult, fill the day with three indoor sights in Takayama (Jinya 60 min, Showa-kan 50 min, Yatai Kaikan 50 min). All are within a 10-minute walk of the old town.
bplan/1/title: Hida no Sato instead of Shirakawa-go
bplan/1/desc: If you couldn't reserve the bus, or snow cancels it, switch to Hida no Sato, a 10-minute bus ride from the station. With 30 gassho houses and activities, it may even be better for kids.
bplan/2/title: With kids, the Gero Gassho Village slide
bplan/2/desc: If the walking at Shirakawa-go is too much, spend half a day at Gero Gassho Village (slide and painting) and a foot bath tour. It is 45 minutes from Takayama by limited express.
bplan/3/title: Hida-Furukawa if you have spare time
bplan/3/desc: If you have a free half day before leaving, take the 15-minute local train to Hida-Furukawa. You can see the carp in the Setogawa Canal and the street of white-walled storehouses in an hour.
bplan/4/title: By rental car, go to Kamikochi
bplan/4/desc: With a car, leave it at the Hirayu Akandana parking lot and take the shuttle to Kamikochi (mid-April to November 15). Doing it on the same day as Shin-Hotaka is tight, so choose just one.
bplan/5/title: If the ropeway is suspended, Hirayu no Mori Onsen
bplan/5/desc: If the Shin-Hotaka Ropeway stops for maintenance or strong winds, get off at Hirayu and spend half a day at Hirayu no Mori with its 16 open-air baths. Buses to Takayama run often.
bplan/6/title: Sake brewery tastings on a rainy day
bplan/6/desc: The breweries in Sanmachi (Harada, Funasaka, Hirase and others) offer indoor tastings, so rain doesn't matter. Visiting three or four takes an hour, and kids can have amazake.
nearby_alternatives/0/reason: When you want to reach Shirakawa-go from the Kanazawa side and give more weight to city sightseeing and food
nearby_alternatives/1/reason: For a short trip where you stay in the transfer city of Nagoya and visit Takayama as a day trip
nearby_alternatives/2/reason: When the Tateyama Alpine Route, the snow walls and Northern Alps scenery are the main goal and you use the direct flight to Toyama Airport
checks/0: Reserve Limited Express Hida seats (peak season and observation seats sell out early)
checks/1: Many Shirakawa-go buses require reservations (Nohibus website)
checks/2: In winter (December to March), bring waterproof shoes, ice cleats and gloves, and allow for bus delays
checks/3: Mountain temperatures swing between morning and evening, so bring a jacket
checks/4: Many morning market stalls and small restaurants accept cash only
checks/5: Old town shops close at 5 p.m., so shop during the day
checks/6: During the Takayama Festival (April 14-15 and October 9-10), lodging fills up a year ahead
checks/7: Check the seasonal closures of the Shin-Hotaka Ropeway and Kamikochi
checks/8: Hot spring inns fix their dinner times, so keep to your check-in time
checks/9: Flights departing from Nagoya (NGO) after 17:00 fit this route
